title: Skiing in Japan for the First Time: An Instructor's Checklist
description: What to pack, rent or buy, what a day costs (median lift pass ¥4,800), lessons, picking a resort, safety and the green-red-black piste code.
html:
Who this is for

I have taught first-timers every winter for years, most of them adults who have never stood on snow. This is the list of things I end up explaining in the first ten minutes of a lesson, written down once. It covers packing, renting, what a day costs, lessons, choosing a resort, the day itself, and safety.

What to pack

Japanese resorts rent almost everything. In YukiNavi, 312 of the 320 resorts with rental data have a rental shop, and several large ones (for example [[gala_yuzawa]], [[karuizawa]], [[furano]], [[ishiuchi_maruyama]]) rent jackets and pants as well. You still need to bring the small items, because rental shops often do not carry them.

  • Base layer top and bottom (synthetic or wool, not cotton) and a fleece mid layer.
  • Waterproof gloves. Thin liner gloves help on cold Hokkaido days.
  • Goggles and a neck gaiter. Sunglasses are not enough in falling snow.
  • One pair of thin ski socks. Thick socks make boots hurt.
  • Sunscreen and lip balm. UV at altitude is strong even in January.
  • Cash. Big resorts take cards; small municipal hills often do not.

Renting vs buying

My opinion as an instructor: rent skis and poles, buy boots first. A rental boot that is half a size wrong is the most common reason a beginner has a bad day, and it is the one piece of equipment that follows you to every resort. Skis matter far less at your level, and rental shops let you swap lengths.

If you ski once a year, rent everything. If you plan three or more days this season, buying boots pays off in comfort before it pays off in money.

What a day costs

Lift pass is リフト券 (rifuto-ken). Of the 403 resorts in YukiNavi, 355 list an adult one-day price. The median is ¥4,800. The middle half of resorts fall between ¥3,140 and ¥6,000. The cheapest listed is ¥300 (a town hill in Hokkaido) and the most expensive is ¥16,700 ([[rusutsu]]). The famous names are well above the median: [[niseko]] ¥13,500, [[hakuba]] ¥9,800, [[nozawa]] ¥7,800.

Rental is the second cost. As one data point, [[karuizawa]] lists an adult ski set at ¥7,500 for the day, ¥7,200 if paid online in advance. Add a lesson, lunch, and the bus or train, and a first day at a major resort is roughly two to three times the lift pass. At a mid-size regional resort it is closer to the pass price doubled.

Whether to take a lesson

Take a half-day group lesson on day one. I say this knowing I am paid to teach, so here is the reason: the first two hours decide whether you learn to stop and turn or learn to fall. Friends who ski are usually bad teachers because they cannot remember how they learned. After a half day you know enough to practice alone on the beginner slope in the afternoon.

English-language lessons exist at 51 resorts in the data, mostly in Niseko, Hakuba, Yuzawa and the resorts run by Prince Hotels. Elsewhere, schools teach in Japanese. A beginner lesson is mostly demonstration and imitation, so it still works, but confirm the language when you book.

How to pick a resort

For a first trip, three things matter more than snow quality.

  1. Access. Shorter is better. Pick a resort you can reach by train and a short shuttle, so the day is not spent in transit. [[gala_yuzawa]] is 71 minutes from Tokyo by shinkansen and the station opens into the resort.
  2. Beginner terrain. YukiNavi shows the beginner, intermediate and advanced share where the resort publishes it. [[karuizawa]] is 58 percent beginner. [[hakuba]] is 30 percent beginner and 50 percent intermediate, which is better for a second trip.
  3. English support. The app rates each resort low, medium or high. High means English-speaking staff and menus. Only 14 resorts are rated high.

Do not pick by reputation. Niseko and Hakuba are famous for powder and long runs, which you cannot use yet, and you pay for them.

The flow of a day

Most resorts run lifts from about 8:30 to 16:00, some later. Arrive before the lifts open. Rental shops queue by 9:00 on weekends, and fitting boots takes longer than you expect. Buy the lift pass online where the resort offers it; 154 resorts in the data have an online ticket page and several sell it slightly cheaper than the window.

Ski two hours, eat early (restaurants fill between 12:00 and 13:00), ski two more hours, and stop while you still have energy. After the lifts close, the onsen, a hot spring bath, is the normal end to the day in most ski towns. Bring a small towel; many onsen rent or sell them but not all.

Safety basics

  • Wear a helmet. Rental shops have them.
  • Stay inside the ropes. Off-piste rules vary by resort and in Hokkaido the forest holds tree wells you can fall into head first.
  • The person below you has right of way. Look uphill before you start.
  • Drink water. Cold air hides how much you sweat.
  • Most injuries happen on the last run. I have seen this every season. Legs are tired, the light is flat, and people take one more run because the pass is paid for. Decide in advance that the second-to-last run is the last one.

The Japanese piste color code

Japan does not use the North American green circle, blue square, black diamond system, nor the European blue, red, black. The standard here is:

ColorJapaneseLevel
Green初級 (shokyu)Beginner
Red中級 (chukyu)Intermediate
Black上級 (jokyu)Advanced

Red in Japan is roughly a North American blue. Grading is relative to the resort, so a green at [[hakuba]] can be steeper than a red at a small local hill. Read the trail map at the base, and ask the lift staff if you are unsure where a lift leads. Many lifts serve only red and black runs with no easy way down.

Information as of November 2026. Prices and operating status change; check the official site before you go.

title: Japanese Ski Resorts with English Lessons and English Support
description: All 51 resorts in YukiNavi with English ski lessons, with prefecture, nearest city, adult day pass and access, plus what the English rating means.
html:
What the English rating in YukiNavi means

Every resort in YukiNavi carries an English support level. It is a judgement about the resort as a whole, not only the ski school.

  • High: English-speaking staff and English menus or signage are normal. 14 of 403 resorts.
  • Medium: some signage and information in English, staff English varies by desk. 84 resorts.
  • Low: limited English support. 305 resorts.

Separately, the school field records whether the ski school offers lessons in English. 51 resorts have this flag. The two do not always line up. [[inawashiro]], [[kuju]] and [[kamui_ski_links]] are rated low overall but run an English or international school. [[rusutsu]] and [[niseko]] are rated high but their school entries in the data are not yet filled in, so they are missing from the table below even though English lessons are easy to find there.

An honest note before the list

I teach at a Japanese resort. Outside Niseko, Hakuba and a handful of destination resorts, the typical ski school has one or two instructors who can run a lesson in English, and they are booked first. Ticket windows, rental shops and restaurants at low-rated resorts work in Japanese. You can manage with a translation app and patience, but do not expect it to be like a Canadian or Austrian resort. If you want everything in English, choose from the high group and accept the price.

How to book

Book the lesson before you book the lift pass. English slots at medium-rated resorts sell out on weekends and over the New Year holiday. If you are a complete beginner, a half-day group lesson is enough for day one.

title: Getting to Japanese Ski Resorts by Train
description: Resorts reachable by shinkansen plus a short shuttle: Echigo-Yuzawa, Karuizawa, Iiyama, Jomo-Kogen and Tohoku, with pass prices and taxi-only warnings.
html:
Why train

Winter roads in Nagano, Niigata and Hokkaido are icy and most rental cars come with studless tires that foreign drivers have never used. The shinkansen (bullet train) runs on time in snow, and the resorts built around it exist because Japanese skiers have been doing day trips from Tokyo for forty years. This article lists the resorts in YukiNavi that you can reach by shinkansen and a short bus, shuttle or walk, and names the ones where you will need a taxi.

How the data was selected

I took resorts marked reachable by public transport in the app whose access text names a shinkansen station, then added the resorts whose nearest station is Echigo-Yuzawa or Jomo-Kogen, both Joetsu Shinkansen stops. Prices are the adult one-day lift pass in the data. Shuttle times are from the resorts' own access pages as recorded in the app.

Tokyo side: Echigo-Yuzawa

Echigo-Yuzawa is the easiest ski station in Japan. In winter the Joetsu Shinkansen continues one stop to Gala-Yuzawa, a station that opens directly into the resort. Most other Yuzawa resorts run free shuttles from the East or West exit.

ResortStationLast legAdult day pass
[[gala_yuzawa]]Gala-Yuzawa (71 min from Tokyo)Walk, station connected¥8,000
[[ipponsugi_snow_park]]Echigo-Yuzawa3 min walk¥2,700
[[naspa_ski_garden]]Echigo-YuzawaShuttle 3 min¥7,000
[[kandatsu_snow_resort]]Echigo-YuzawaFree shuttle 7 min, daily¥6,800
[[ishiuchi_maruyama]]Echigo-YuzawaFree shuttle 10 min, East Exit¥8,500
[[yuzawa_park]]Echigo-YuzawaFree shuttle 10 min¥4,500
[[iwappara]]Echigo-YuzawaFree shuttle 6-16 min (weekends); reserved loop bus weekdays¥5,500
[[yuzawa_nakazato]]Echigo-YuzawaFree shuttle 15 min, West Exit; or local train to Echigo-Nakazato¥6,700
[[kagura]]Echigo-YuzawaRoute bus 18 min¥8,500
[[maiko_snow_resort]]Echigo-YuzawaFree shuttle 20-30 min¥7,300

[[naeba]] is also in the Yuzawa area, but its shuttle from the station is for hotel guests and the app notes a taxi at about ¥11,000. Day visitors should use the direct bus from Tokyo listed in the app (about 2 hours).

Tokyo side: Karuizawa and the Hokuriku Shinkansen

The Hokuriku Shinkansen passes Karuizawa, Nagano and Iiyama. Karuizawa is the shortest ski trip from Tokyo by train.

ResortStationLast legAdult day pass
[[karuizawa]]Karuizawa (about 1h10m from Tokyo incl. shuttle)10 min walk or free shuttle from South Exit¥10,000
[[nozawa]]IiyamaNozawa Onsen Liner direct bus; free village shuttle to the slopes¥7,800
[[togari_onsen]]IiyamaShuttle 20 min, 5 round trips daily¥5,800
[[romance_no_kamisama]]IiyamaFree shuttle 20 min, daily¥6,200
[[kijima_snow_park]]IiyamaShuttle from stop 4; few runs on weekdays¥5,000
[[madarao_kogen]]IiyamaBus to Madarao Kogen; NOTOMA shuttle ¥1,400¥9,000
[[itoigawa_seaside_valley]]ItoigawaLocal bus about 50 min, ¥670¥5,000

Hakuba is reached from Nagano station by express bus, about 1 hour to [[hakuba47]] and 1 hour 15 minutes to [[hakuba_goryu]]. It works as a train trip but the bus leg is not short. [[shiga]] is a direct Nagaden bus from Nagano station East Exit.

Tokyo side: Jomo-Kogen and Minakami

Jomo-Kogen is the Joetsu Shinkansen stop before the Yuzawa tunnel. The Gunma resorts behind it are quieter and cheaper than Yuzawa, but the last legs are longer and several shuttles need a reservation.

ResortStationLast legAdult day pass
[[mt_t_hoshino]]Jomo-KogenDirect bus about 35 min¥9,000
[[norn_minakami]]Jomo-KogenReserved shuttle about 30 min; or free shuttle 20 min from Minakami Sta.¥6,300
[[kawaba]]Jomo-KogenFree reserved shuttle, one departure at 8:00¥7,900
[[minakami_kogen_fujiwara]]Jomo-KogenRoute bus about 50 min¥4,500
[[minakami_kogen]]Jomo-KogenPaid reserved shuttle about 70 min¥5,500

[[katashina_kogen]] and [[snowpark_oze_tokura]] are also served by route bus from Jomo-Kogen, but the ride is 1 hour 40 minutes to 2 hours. Treat them as overnight trips.

Tohoku and Hokkaido by shinkansen

ResortStationLast legAdult day pass
[[zao_raiza]]Kaminoyama-Onsen (Yamagata Shinkansen)Free White Echo shuttle 30 min, 2 round trips a day¥5,000
[[zao_sarukura]]Kaminoyama-OnsenFree shuttle¥4,500
[[hanagasa_kogen]]Oishida (Yamagata Shinkansen)Bus 45 min or taxi 25 min¥1,900
[[tazawako]]Tazawako (Akita Shinkansen)Local bus 30 min or taxi 20 min¥5,800
[[appi]]Morioka, then JR Hanawa Line 1 h to Appi-KogenArea shuttle from Appi-Kogen Sta.¥9,500
[[aomori_spring]]Shin-AomoriReserved Aomori Spring Liner shuttle¥9,400

[[zao]] itself is a bus from Yamagata station, about 40 minutes. In Hokkaido the shinkansen ends at Hakodate, so Sapporo-area resorts are reached by plane plus bus. [[tomamu]] has its own JR station served by limited express trains from Sapporo, with a free 5 to 10 minute shuttle.

Where you will need a taxi

Many smaller resorts sit 5 to 40 minutes from a local station with no bus. YukiNavi marks 16 resorts as taxi-only from the station and another 10 as having no public transport option listed. Examples with the taxi time from the app:

  • [[chateraise_nobeyama]]: 5 min from Nobeyama Sta., about ¥1,500-1,600.
  • [[kurohime_kogen]]: 10 min from Kurohime Sta.
  • [[niseko_moiwa]]: 10 min from Niseko Sta.
  • [[yomase_onsen]]: 12 min from Yudanaka Sta.
  • [[xjam_takaifuji]]: 20 min from Yudanaka Sta.
  • [[yunomaru]]: 25 min from Shigeno Sta.; the bus route was discontinued.
  • [[minenohara_kogen]]: 35 min from Ueda Sta.
  • [[kirigamine_family]]: 40 min from Kami-Suwa Sta.

Rural taxis are not waiting at every station. Ask your accommodation to book one, or call the number posted at the station. Agree on a pick-up time for the return, because the last local train leaves early and you will have skis.

Practical points

  • Reserve shinkansen seats for weekend mornings in January and February; the Tokyo to Echigo-Yuzawa trains fill with skiers.
  • Oversize baggage rules apply on the Tokaido, Sanyo and Kyushu shinkansen. Skis in a bag are allowed on the Joetsu and Hokuriku lines, but put them in the space behind the last row.
  • Where the app says reservation required for a shuttle, it means the day before at the latest. Several Gunma and Fukushima shuttles do not run at all without bookings.
  • Check the return shuttle time before you buy the lift pass. At a two-round-trip resort, missing the afternoon bus means a long taxi.

Information as of November 2026. Prices and operating status change; check the official site before you go.

title: Lift Pass Prices in Japan 2026-27: What to Expect
description: Adult day-pass prices at 355 Japanese resorts: median ¥4,800, bands by region, Niseko and Hakuba vs the median, online discounts, student and Yukimaji deals.
html:
The short version

A lift pass is リフト券 (rifuto-ken). Across the 355 resorts in YukiNavi that list an adult one-day price, the median is ¥4,800. Half of all resorts charge between ¥3,140 and ¥6,000. The resorts foreign visitors have heard of charge two to three and a half times the median. Of the 403 resorts, 186 have confirmed 2026-27 prices; the rest still carry last season's figure until the resort publishes an update, so treat them as a floor.

Price bands

Adult one-day passResortsWhat you get
Under ¥4,000125Municipal and town hills, a few lifts, often one base lodge. Many are cash only.
¥4,000-4,99964Regional resorts with 5 to 15 courses, basic rental and a school in Japanese.
¥5,000-5,99971Mid-size resorts near Nagano, Niigata and Gifu, usually with a bus from a station.
¥6,000-6,99950Larger regional resorts and most Kanto day-trip resorts.
¥7,000-7,99918Established names such as [[nozawa]], [[zao]] (¥8,000 just above), [[hakuba_iwatake]].
¥8,000-9,99918Destination resorts: [[hakuba]], [[shiga]], [[appi]], [[furano]], [[myoko]], [[naeba]], [[gala_yuzawa]].
¥10,000 and up9Niseko area, [[rusutsu]], [[karuizawa]], [[hakuba_goryu]], [[hakuba47]].

By region

The regional medians below are from the resorts with a listed adult price. Hokkaido has both the cheapest and the most expensive resorts in the country, so its median says little about the resorts you are likely to visit.

RegionResorts with priceCheapestMedianMost expensive
Hokkaido77¥300¥3,100¥16,700
Tohoku84¥930¥3,500¥9,500
Hokuriku (Toyama, Ishikawa, Fukui)17¥1,560¥4,000¥6,200
Chugoku17¥500¥4,500¥6,800
Kansai22¥1,000¥4,850¥6,800
Niigata43¥1,500¥5,000¥9,800
Nagano56¥2,610¥5,600¥10,000
Chubu (Gifu, Shizuoka, Yamanashi)15¥1,040¥5,600¥6,900
Kanto21¥4,000¥6,300¥9,000

Kanto is the most expensive region on median because every resort there is a Tokyo day trip and priced for it. Tohoku is the best value for the terrain you get: [[zao]] at ¥8,000 and [[appi]] at ¥9,500 are the top of the region, and the prefectural median in Yamagata is ¥3,450.

The cheapest and the most expensive

The three cheapest passes in the data are town-run hills in northern Hokkaido: [[rishiri_tenbozan]] ¥300, [[nakagawa_chomin]] ¥400, [[sarufutsu_sonei]] ¥500. They have one or two lifts and exist for local schoolchildren. They are not a destination, but they show what a lift ride costs when nobody is paying for a resort village.

The top of the list is all Hokkaido and Nagano: [[rusutsu]] ¥16,700, [[niseko]] (All Mountain Pass) ¥13,500, [[niseko_moiwa]] ¥13,000, [[niseko_grand_hirafu]] and [[niseko_hanazono]] ¥12,500, [[niseko_village]] ¥10,700, then [[karuizawa]], [[hakuba_goryu]] and [[hakuba47]] at ¥10,000.

How the famous resorts compare

ResortAdult day passMultiple of national median (¥4,800)
[[rusutsu]]¥16,7003.5x
[[niseko]]¥13,5002.8x
[[hakuba]] (Happo-one)¥9,8002.0x
[[furano]]¥9,0001.9x
[[zao]]¥8,0001.7x
[[nozawa]]¥7,8001.6x

Niseko and Rusutsu use seasonal pricing. The app records the peak-season window price. The deals data shows the Niseko United pass at ¥8,800 at the window in early season against ¥13,500 from December 24 to February 28, so the date you travel changes the price by more than any discount.

My view as an instructor: for a first or second week on skis, the ¥5,000 to ¥7,000 band buys more useful skiing per yen than Niseko does. You pay the Niseko premium for off-piste access and an English-speaking town, not for the beginner slope.

Buying online

154 of the 403 resorts have an online ticket page recorded in YukiNavi. The discount for buying in advance is usually small but consistent:

  • [[niseko]] All Mountain Pass: ¥12,800 online against ¥13,500 at the window in peak season, about 5 percent. A ¥500 key card fee applies on the first purchase.
  • [[gala_yuzawa]]: ¥7,500 online, ¥8,000 at the window.
  • [[karuizawa]]: ¥9,500 online, ¥10,000 at the window in the main season; ¥7,500 to December 18.
  • [[sapporo_kokusai]]: ¥6,700 online, ¥7,000 at the window.
  • [[furano]]: ¥500 off at the web price.
  • [[kiroro]]: 5 percent off on the official web store.

Early-bird tickets sold before the season are the bigger saving. In the deals data: [[hakuba_iwatake]] ¥5,700 (normally ¥7,500), [[manza]] ¥4,500 (normally ¥6,300), [[hunter]] ¥4,200 (normally ¥6,500). Most close at the end of November. The [[hakuba]] early-bird at ¥6,400 instead of ¥9,800 requires a Japanese My Number Card, so it is for residents only.

Many online tickets are issued through QR codes at a self-service machine at the resort, and some vendors (Webket, Asoview, WAmazing) have English pages. Buy by the day before where the app says so; dynamic-priced resorts like [[ishiuchi_maruyama]] change the web price daily.

Student and youth prices

85 resorts list a separate student price. The median saving against the adult pass is ¥1,200, about 22 percent. Examples: [[shiga]] ¥6,500 against ¥9,500, [[niseko]] ¥11,500 against ¥13,500, [[rusutsu]] ¥12,500 against ¥16,700, [[ishiuchi_maruyama]] ¥4,200 against ¥8,500 on its online student plan. A student card from any country is normally accepted, but Japanese staff may not recognise it; carry a passport as well.

Yukimaji: free lifts at 19 to 22

Yukimaji (雪マジ) is a Recruit programme that gives people aged 19 to 22 (born April 2, 2004 to April 1, 2008) free one-day passes at 130 participating resorts, up to two times per resort, with discounts after that. It runs from November 5 until each resort closes. You register with a Recruit ID on Jalan and the Maji-bu site, verify by SMS, and show the coupon with original photo ID at the window. The SMS step needs a phone that can receive Japanese verification messages, so in practice it is built for residents and exchange students. If you are studying in Japan at the right age, it is the single biggest saving in the data.

Prince Snow Resorts runs a separate scheme: anyone born April 2, 2006 to April 1, 2007 rides free on weekdays at eight Prince resorts including [[furano]], [[naeba]], [[kagura]], [[karuizawa]], [[shiga]] (Yakebitai) and [[manza]], from November 30 to April 30, excluding weekends, holidays and the New Year period. It uses a coupon in the Seibu Prince Global Rewards app plus photo ID.

What to budget

For a regional resort with a train connection, plan on ¥5,000 to ¥7,000 for the pass. For Hakuba, Shiga or Myoko, ¥9,000 to ¥10,000. For Niseko in peak season, ¥12,500 to ¥13,500 for a one-mountain or all-mountain pass. Rusutsu is in its own band. Buy online where offered, travel outside December 24 to February 28 if you can, and if you are a student bring the card.
